claims.claim: The SOP attaches an Oxygen Solubility at Indicated Pressure chart tabulating oxygen solubility against temperature for barometric pressures from 760 down to 730 mm Hg.

chunks.locator: Attachment, "Oxygen Solubility at Indicated Pressure" chart, 760-730 mm Hg block plus the head of the 725-690 mm Hg block (tail of the Table 1 calibration log precedes it)

claims.claim: In the attached Oxygen Solubility at Indicated Pressure chart the barometric pressure columns are labelled in both millimetres and inches of mercury (760 mm Hg corresponds to 29.92 in Hg) and the tabulated solubility values are in milligrams per litre.

The EPA oxygen-solubility chart gives dissolved-oxygen saturation at 20 degrees C as 9.06 mg/L at 760 mm Hg, falling to 8.69 mg/L at 730 mm Hg, so the saturation value a calibration is checked against depends jointly on water temperature and barometric pressure.
The EPA oxygen-solubility chart gives dissolved-oxygen saturation at 25 degrees C as 8.24 mg/L at 760 mm Hg and 7.90 mg/L at 730 mm Hg.
The EPA oxygen-solubility chart gives dissolved-oxygen saturation at 0 degrees C as 14.57 mg/L at 760 mm Hg, the highest value in the chart.
The EPA oxygen-solubility chart runs to 45 degrees C, where saturation is 5.94 mg/L at 760 mm Hg, and gives no value for water warmer than 45 degrees C.
A continuation of the EPA oxygen-solubility chart covers barometric pressures from 725 down to 690 mm Hg (28.54 to 27.17 in Hg), extending the chart below the 730 mm Hg limit of the first block.
In the low-pressure continuation of the EPA oxygen-solubility chart, saturation at 0 degrees C is 13.89 mg/L at 725 mm Hg and 13.22 mg/L at 690 mm Hg, reported in mg/L.

Across the EPA oxygen-solubility chart the saturation value decreases both as water temperature rises and as barometric pressure falls, so dissolved-oxygen calibration cannot be judged without the concurrent temperature and pressure readings.

The Oxygen Solubility at Indicated Pressure chart attached to the EPA SOP is taken from the Draft EPA Handbook of Methods for Acid Deposition Studies, Field Operations for Surface Water Chemistry, EPA/600/4-89/020, August 1989.

gaps: States no acceptance criterion for the initial calibration of any parameter except dissolved oxygen: pH, specific conductance, ORP and turbidity are all judged against unspecified 'instrument specifications' or the manufacturer's manual, so the SOP alone cannot tell an operator whether a calibration passed.

Gives no pH electrode slope or millivolt criterion (no percent-of-theoretical-slope window and no mV-per-pH-unit range); the only pH number in the document is the plus or minus 0.3 pH unit post-calibration criterion measured with the pH 7 buffer.

States no temperature accuracy requirement of its own. Plus or minus 0.2 degrees C appears only as an example of 'the accuracy of the sensor', and temperature is the one parameter absent from the Table of default post calibration criteria, so no drift limit for a temperature sensor exists in this SOP.

Does not reproduce the ORP Zobell millivolt-versus-temperature correction table; it directs the operator to the table on the standard bottle or its instruction sheet, so no ORP calibration value can be looked up from this document at any temperature.

Names no turbidity standard values beyond a zero or 0.02 NTU low standard and an unspecified 'high' standard, so the SOP does not say what NTU standards a turbidity calibration must use or how far apart they must be.
Defines specific conductance as conductivity corrected to 25 degrees C but gives no temperature-compensation coefficient, correction equation, or check that the instrument's compensation is working.

Gives no deployment duration or mid-deployment check interval for continuously deployed sondes; it says only that they are calibrated before deployment and checked on recovery. The drift and post-calibration criteria are not simply left to the project QAPP: section 6.0 defers to the quality assurance project plan or sampling and analysis plan first, but supplies its own default post calibration criteria for when that plan does not specify one (dissolved oxygen plus or minus 0.5 mg/L of the saturation value, specific conductance plus 5 percent of standard or plus 10 uS/cm whichever is greater, pH plus or minus 0.3 pH unit with the pH 7 buffer, turbidity plus 5 percent of standard, ORP plus or minus 10 mV).

The attached Oxygen Solubility at Indicated Pressure chart is for fresh water only: it tabulates solubility against temperature and barometric pressure with no salinity, chloride, or conductivity correction, so it cannot be used to check a DO calibration in brackish or saline water.

The oxygen-solubility chart covers 0 to 45 degrees C and 760 down to 690 mm Hg only; no saturation value is given for water above 45 degrees C or for barometric pressure below 690 mm Hg (roughly 3,000 ft and above).
Prescribes no significant-figures, rounding, or units-reporting convention for any of the six parameters, and no required resolution for recorded field readings.

Says calibration standards must not be expired and should be near ambient temperature, but gives no standard storage temperature, no shelf life, and no rule for how long an opened bottle of pH buffer, Zobell solution or conductivity standard may be used.

Covers calibration only: it gives no measurement-stabilization criterion in the environmental sample (no 'readings stable within X for Y minutes'), no purge criteria, and no guidance on the order in which parameters are read.
